transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you’re here. What brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because my husband wanted me to come, but honestly, I'm just hoping someone will finally actually listen to me. It's been months. Months and months of this, and I am just exhausted trying to get people to understand what is going on right under our noses. 

It’s his family. My husband's family. They are... they are quietly messing with our money, and not just our money, our good name in the community. And I know how people react when I say that, they get that look on their face, but you have to understand—I am a billing clerk. I work with invoices and accounts all day long, I've been doing it for years, and I am very, very careful with my numbers. So when these little billing errors start showing up at work—just out of nowhere, these tiny discrepancies, a misplaced decimal here, a missing file there, things that specifically make it look like I don't know what I'm doing or that I'm slipping up—I know it's not me making those mistakes. Somebody is tampering with it. 

And it’s not just at the office, it spills over into everything else. We go to church on Sundays, we've been going to the same congregation for over a decade, and suddenly people are acting funny toward me. People who used to ask me to help with the bake sale are looking at me sideways, whispering when I walk into the fellowship hall, treating me like I'm some kind of thief or liar. It’s a coordinated effort to ice me out and ruin my reputation. 

And the most frustrating part, the part that makes me want to pull my hair out, is that no matter what records anyone pulls up—whether it's the IT logs at my job or our own financial statements—they always have some convenient excuse. They say, "Oh, it's a computer glitch," or "Oh, you're just imagining things, people are just busy." But I know. I know it ties back to them. His family has never liked me, and they are orchestrating all of this behind the scenes to drain us dry and make me look crazy, and I just need someone to look at the facts and see what they are doing.
Have you heard or seen things that other people around you do not, such as voices when no one is there?

No, no, I... I don't hear voices. Nothing like that. I know exactly why you're asking, believe me, I've seen the way people look at me when I try to explain all this, like they're waiting for me to say I'm talking to ghosts or something. But no, I don't hear people speaking when no one is there, and I don't see visions. 

I deal with numbers. I deal with hard facts, day in and day out, and I have since I got out of high school. That's what a billing clerk does, you know? You have to be grounded. You have to look at the black and white on the screen, the actual data, so you can balance the ledgers. So I'm not imagining things, and I'm definitely not hearing things in my head. The things I'm talking about—the whispering at the fellowship hall, the missing files at the office—those are real people doing real things. 

It's not some trick of the mind. It's just that they are so incredibly careful about how they do it. Like last Tuesday, for example, I was looking at a vendor account, an account I have managed perfectly without a single hitch since 2019, and suddenly there's a routing error. A routing error! Out of the blue. I don't need to hear imaginary voices to know someone went into the system and changed the code just to make me look incompetent to my supervisor. I just need my own two eyes to see the screen. So no, no voices. Just the reality of what they're doing to me, which is bad enough without people thinking I'm making it up in my head.
Have you generally been this suspicious and on guard toward other people for most of your adult life?

No, no, not at all. That's the thing, that's what makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating. If you had asked anyone who knows me—well, anyone who knew me before all this started, I mean—they would tell you I was the most trusting person. Too trusting, honestly. My husband used to tease me about it when we first got married, back when things were normal. He'd say, "You'd give the shirt off your back to a stranger," and he was right. I was always the one organizing the office potlucks, always the one volunteering to stay late to help a new hire figure out the billing software, because I just... I believed people were basically good, you know? 

I never spent my life looking over my shoulder. Never. I mean, I've worked in the same office for fifteen years, I've lived in the same neighborhood for twelve, and I never had an issue with anyone until his family decided they had a problem with me. I wasn't the kind of person who double-checked every lock or worried about what people were saying behind my back. I was just living my life, doing my job, paying my taxes. 

It’s only recently, since this whole coordinated effort began, that I’ve had to be on guard. And who wouldn't be? When you start seeing your own work tampered with, when you see people you've known for a decade suddenly whispering and pointing when you walk into church, you have to protect yourself. It's not paranoia if they're actually doing it. It's just self-preservation. But before this? No. I was never like this. I was just a normal, trusting person who went to work and came home, and I just want to get back to that. I just want them to stop so I can go back to being the person I was.
When did you first start believing that your husband’s family was targeting you in this way?

Well, let me think... it’s been about nine months now. Yes, nine months, because it all started right around the holidays last year, and you know how stressful that time of year can be anyway, but this was... this was different. 

We had this huge, just awful disagreement with his family. It started out being about holiday expectations—who was hosting, who was expected to travel, the usual things that families bicker about, but then they brought up money. They started making these little comments, these passive-aggressive remarks about how we spend our money, how we manage our household, and it just spiraled from there. It was so incredibly tense. My husband’s sister said some things that were just completely out of line, and his mother, well, she’s never really approved of me, but she made it very clear that she felt I wasn't handling our finances properly, which is rich, considering I do this for a living! 

Anyway, it was right after that whole blowout that things started happening. That’s when the first billing error showed up at work, right after we got back from that terrible holiday visit. At first, I thought, okay, I’m just stressed, maybe I did hit the wrong key. But then it happened again a week later. And then the week after that. And then the whispering at church started right around February. So yes, it’s been about nine solid months of this constant, relentless... campaign against me. Nine months of checking everything three times, looking over my shoulder, trying to figure out how they’re getting into my system and who they're talking to at the congregation. It’s exhausting, it really is, but I know exactly when it started, because it all ties perfectly back to that argument over the holidays. They decided they were going to punish me, and they haven't stopped since.
Before the past nine months, did you ever have similar suspicions that other people were trying to harm, cheat, or deceive you?

No, no, never. Like I said, I was always so trusting. I mean, I’ve been trying to rack my brain, trying to think if there was ever a time before this where I felt like people were out to get me, and there really wasn’t. I mean, sure, everyone has moments, right? Like, maybe you think a cashier shortchanged you on purpose, or you wonder if a coworker took credit for your idea, but nothing like this. Nothing coordinated. Nothing where I felt like someone was actively trying to ruin my life or my reputation. 

Before this whole mess with his family started, I was just... normal. I would go to work, do my job, come home, make dinner, maybe watch a little TV. I didn't spend my time wondering if someone was hacking into my billing software. I didn't spend my Sundays scanning the pews at church to see who was whispering about me. It just wasn't on my radar. I mean, why would it be? I’m just a regular person. I don’t have some dark past or anything. I’ve lived a very quiet, very boring life, honestly. 

And that’s why this is all so shocking to me. It’s like I woke up one day in someone else’s life, a life where I have to double-check every single keystroke, where I have to keep a log of everything that goes wrong at the office just to prove I’m not losing my mind or, worse, incompetent. Because that’s what they want, isn't it? They want my supervisor to think I can't do my job. They want the people at church to think I'm some kind of... I don't know, some kind of unstable person. But before nine months ago? No. I never worried about people trying to harm me or cheat me. I was just living my life. I really wish I could just go back to that.
Before these past nine months, did you ever have trouble trusting people or suspect that others were trying to take advantage of you?

Well, like I was just saying, no. I really didn't. I mean, I know I'm repeating myself, but it's just the honest truth. Before this past year, I never had any trouble trusting anyone. I never thought people were trying to take advantage of me. 

I mean, I'm trying to be really thorough here, trying to give you the whole picture, because I know you're trying to figure this out, but I keep coming back to the same answer. I was just... I was easygoing. I really was. If someone asked me for a favor, I did it. If someone needed to borrow five dollars for the vending machine at work, I handed it over and didn't even keep track of whether they paid me back. That's just how I operated. I didn't have this... this filter, I guess you'd call it, where I was constantly analyzing people's motives. 

I remember this one time, maybe five or six years ago, a roofer came by the house after a bad storm and said we needed some shingles replaced. My husband was out of town, and the guy said he could do it right then for a cash discount. I just handed him the money. Didn't ask for a license, didn't call around for quotes. My husband was furious when he got back, said I got scammed, but the guy actually did fix the roof! So, you see? I just assumed people were honest. I assumed they were straightforward. 

I didn't have any reason to think otherwise, because, well, why would people waste their time trying to pull one over on me? I'm just a billing clerk. I don't have some massive inheritance, I don't have some high-profile job. I'm just me. So no, before his family decided to make it their mission to destroy my credibility, I never had any issues with trust. I trusted everyone. Maybe that was my mistake, honestly. Maybe if I hadn't been so trusting, I would have seen this coming. I would have noticed the signs earlier, before they got so deep into my life and my computer and my church. But I didn't. Because I just didn't think like that. I really, really didn't.
Before the past nine months, were there ever other times in your adult life when you were very suspicious of people’s motives or felt they were out to get you?

I feel like you're asking me the exact same question just using different words now, Doctor. I mean, I know you have to be thorough, I do, but I really don't know how many different ways I can say no. 

Are you trying to find something specific in my past? Because I promise you, if you look at my whole adult life, there is just nothing there. When I was in my twenties, right out of high school, I worked at this little local hardware store before I got into the billing side of things, and I used to leave my purse just sitting right out on the breakroom counter. Wide open sometimes! Anyone could have walked off with it, but I never once thought, you know, "Oh, my coworker is going to steal my wallet," or "The manager is trying to set me up to get fired." I just went in, did my shifts, and went home. 

And then when I met my husband in my thirties, I just... I completely embraced his family. I really did try. I never suspected they had these kinds of vicious ulterior motives back then. I thought we were just a regular family. I never looked at his mother or his sister and thought they were plotting to ruin my career, you know? I didn't spend my thirties or my early forties looking over my shoulder or analyzing every little conversation to see if someone was out to get me. I just went to work, entered my invoices, paid our bills, went to Sunday services... 

I was completely, one hundred percent oblivious to how cruel people could be until they started messing with my billing system and turning the congregation against me nine months ago. So, no, looking back at my entire adult life, there were absolutely no other times I felt like this. I was perfectly fine, perfectly trusting, just living a completely ordinary life until they decided to ruin it.
Outside of these recent nine months, have you ever had trouble keeping close relationships because you felt other people were not to be trusted?

Honestly, Doctor, I feel like we are just going in circles now. It really seems like you’re trying to paint a picture of me as this... this lifelong paranoid loner who just pushes everyone away, and that is just not who I am. Or who I was. Before all this started nine months ago, I had absolutely no trouble keeping close relationships. None at all. 

I mean, take my friend Diane, for example. We’ve known each other since my early thirties, back when I first started doing posting work for this small dental clinic across town. We used to get lunch together every single Tuesday without fail. We’d go to this little deli down the street, split a turkey club—well, actually, I’d usually get the potato soup because their sourdough was always a little too hard for my teeth, but you know what I mean. We talked about everything. Our husbands, our grocery budgets, whatever was on sale at the department store. I never once sat across from Diane and thought, you know, that she was going to use my words against me. I never felt like I had to hide things from her or that she wasn't to be trusted. We were just best friends. 

And it was the exact same way with my neighbors, and the other women in my congregation. We’d do the church bake sales together, we’d organize the summer potlucks. I used to leave my spare house key with the woman next door, Mrs. Gable, whenever my husband and I went down to Myrtle Beach for our vacation every August. You don't just hand over the keys to your front door to someone you think is untrustworthy, right? I trusted her to water my ferns and bring in the mail, and she did, and that was that. I never worried she was going through my drawers or copying my financial documents. 

So, no. I really don't know why we keep coming back to this. I was a good friend, a good neighbor. I didn't have any trouble keeping people in my life, and I certainly didn't ruin my relationships because of trust issues. It's only recently that my social life has been turned upside down, and that is entirely because of what his family is doing to isolate me, not because of some problem I've always had. Before they started this campaign against me, my relationships were perfectly fine.
Have you ever, since your teens or early adulthood, tended to believe that other people were watching you, talking about you, or trying to deceive you?

Doctor, I... I really don't understand why we are still stuck on this. It's like you're trying to dig up something from thirty years ago that just isn't there. When I was a teenager? Heavens, no. I was just a completely normal girl, worrying about normal teenage things. I mean, sure, if I got a bad haircut—which, believe me, happened, my mother used to take me to this awful discount salon next to the grocery store where they just chopped it all off—I might have thought kids in the cafeteria were giggling at my bangs. But that's just being sixteen, right? Everyone feels a little self-conscious at that age. But that's not what you mean. I never thought anyone was actually *watching* me, or trying to deceive me, or plotting against me. 

And in my early adulthood? Like I was saying about the hardware store earlier, I was just working. I was learning how to do the bookkeeping, balancing the daily till, figuring out how to be an adult. I didn't have the time or the energy to sit around thinking people were talking about me behind my back. I was too busy trying to pay off my used car. It was this old blue Honda, and the alternator kept going out, so I had to pick up extra shifts just to cover the mechanic bills. I was focused on practical things, you know? Paying rent, buying groceries, getting to work on time. 

So, no, absolutely not. I never had this... this tendency to think people were deceiving me. Not in my teens, not in my twenties, not in my thirties or most of my forties. I was completely trusting. I just lived my life, day in and day out, doing my billing work and going to church. It is only—and I really need you to hear this, Doctor—it is *only* since his family started this whole campaign to ruin me nine months ago that I've had to be on guard. Before they started messing with my life and spreading lies, I never, ever felt like people were watching me.

Before these past nine months, did you ever hold any strongly fixed beliefs that other people were cheating on you, plotting against you, or trying to harm you, even if others told you there was no evidence?

Doctor, I... I really just don't know how to make this any clearer to you. No. Absolutely not. Before nine months ago, I never had any thoughts like that, because nothing like that was happening to me. I was just living my normal life. 

The whole reason I am sitting in this chair right now, the only reason I am even here talking to you, is because for months now I’ve been trying—just pleading, really—to get people to understand what is actually going on *now*. It is my husband’s family. They are quietly, methodically messing with our money and our good name, and it is driving me to my wit's end because nobody will just open their eyes and look at what they're doing. 

It’s in the details, Doctor. I do billing for a living. I have for years. I know how a ledger is supposed to look, I know how the software routes the invoices, so I know when something is off. Suddenly, out of nowhere, these little billing errors start showing up at work. Things I supposedly entered wrong, or payments that get delayed, just tiny little discrepancies that make me look incompetent. And it's not just the money, it's my reputation. I go to church, a church I have attended for years, and suddenly someone there acts funny toward me. They’ll look away when I walk down the aisle, or they'll whisper over by the coffee urns in the fellowship hall, and I know exactly where the rumors came from. 

And you talk about evidence, about people telling me there's no evidence—that is exactly what I've been dealing with! My boss, my husband, they’ll say, "Oh, it's just a system glitch," or "Oh, the congregation isn't talking about you, you're just stressed." They'll pull up the system logs or the IT reports and try to show me that it was just a computer error. But they don't see the bigger picture. No matter what records anyone pulls up, no matter what they try to point to on a screen to prove me wrong, I *know* it ties back to his family. I know they are the ones orchestrating it. So, no, I didn't spend my whole life thinking people were plotting against me. I'm only saying it now because it is actually happening, and I just need someone to finally believe me.
Outside of this situation with your husband’s family, do you generally mistrust or question other people’s motives in day-to-day life?

No, Doctor. Honestly, I... I feel like a broken record here. Outside of his family, my life is just completely normal. I don't have any reason to question what regular people are doing. 

I mean, take the grocery store, for instance. I go to the same supermarket every Sunday after church, and I always try to get in Chloe’s lane. She’s this sweet young girl with thick glasses who works the register, always talking about her tabby cat. If she accidentally double-scans a can of crushed tomatoes or something, I don't stand there thinking she’s trying to steal from me or trick me. I just figure the scanner beeped twice or she was distracted, you know? I just point it out, she fixes it, and we go back to talking about her cat. I don't question her motives. 

And it’s the same thing at work. If one of the office managers asks me to pull a batch of old invoices from last quarter, I don't sit at my desk wondering *why* they want them or if it’s some kind of trap to get me fired. I just pull the invoices. I do the billing, I process the forms, I do my job. Or like with my hairdresser—I go to Maria now, over on 4th Street, not the awful discount place my mother used to take me to. Maria is wonderful, she has these two little boys who play soccer. When I sit in her chair, I don't worry she’s going to ruin my layers on purpose or that she has some hidden agenda. I just relax and let her cut my hair. 

I trust the mailman, I trust the crossing guard, I trust the people I pass on the street. If someone cuts me off in traffic on my way to the clinic, I just assume they’re running late for work, not that they’re out to get me. So, no. I don't have this general mistrust of the world. The world is fine. Most people are just trying to get through their day, same as me. It is literally *only* his family. If it weren't for what they are specifically doing to me, I wouldn't have a single worry in the world about anyone's motives.
Have you had any experiences that seem impossible or clearly against reality, like being controlled, implanted with thoughts, or receiving special messages meant only for you?

What? No, of course not. Doctor, I... I honestly don't even know where you're getting these ideas. Controlled? Like by microchips or something you see in a movie? Heavens, no. 

My thoughts are entirely my own. I mean, sometimes I wish I could turn them off, especially at night when I'm lying in bed trying to figure out how to fix the mess his family is making of our lives, but they are *my* thoughts. Nobody is putting them in my head. I just lie there, staring at the ceiling fan—it’s one of those Hunter fans, the one with the little frosted glass domes, we put it in about five years ago because our upstairs gets just impossibly stuffy in August—and I just think about my day. Just normal worries about bills and work and what I need to get done the next morning. 

And special messages? From where? The television? I watch the local news at six, usually channel 4 with David and Susan, and then maybe Wheel of Fortune while I fold the laundry in the living room. When David reads the news, he's just reading the news to the whole city. He's not blinking in code at me or trying to send me a secret signal. If he says it's going to rain, I just make sure I put my umbrella in the passenger seat of my car. 

I'm a billing clerk, Doctor. I deal with numbers and spreadsheets and paper invoices all day long. I live in the real world. Two plus two is four, a past-due notice means a thirty-day cycle has passed, a routing number tells the bank where the money goes... everything in my life is completely ordinary and based in reality. I don't believe in magic or sci-fi mind control or people beaming things into my brain. I really feel like you're trying to make me sound crazy with these questions. The only messages I get are the passive-aggressive emails from his sister, and those aren't secret or impossible at all, they're just plain mean. So, no, nothing like that. Nothing impossible. Just the very real, very frustrating things I've already been trying to explain to you.
Before these past nine months, did you often think other people might be out to harm, cheat, or take advantage of you?

Doctor, I really feel like we just went over this a few minutes ago. Are you getting all this down in your notes? Because I want to make sure I am being absolutely clear. No. Before nine months ago, I never had a single thought that anyone was out to get me or cheat me or take advantage of me in any way shape or form. 

Like I said, I have been working in billing and posting for years and years. Actually, I started doing data entry right out of high school for a local plumbing supply company. Reynolds and Sons, they were called. They went under back in two thousand and eight when the housing market crashed, which was a shame because old Mr. Reynolds was a sweetheart, but anyway, I handled all their purchase orders. If a vendor overcharged us, or if a driver claimed he worked four hours of overtime when he only worked two, I never once sat there and thought they were doing it to personally attack me or ruin my life. I just assumed they were bad at math or trying to squeeze an extra twenty bucks out of the company, not that they had some grand plot against me. 

I have always been a trusting person. I used to be the one who would collect all the cash for the teacher appreciation gifts when my daughter was in middle school. I would hold onto hundreds of dollars in a manila envelope in my kitchen drawer, and nobody ever thought I was cheating them, and I never thought the other mothers were trying to set me up or take advantage of my time. We all just got along. I was the one organizing the neighborhood potlucks, for heaven's sake. You do not do that if you think everyone is out to harm you. 

So I really need you to understand that this is not some lifelong personality flaw of mine. I am not a suspicious person by nature. I was perfectly happy and perfectly trusting until exactly nine months ago when my husband's family decided to start messing with my life and my accounts. Before that? Nothing. Not a single worry.
Have you ever, at any point before these past nine months, had a recurring pattern of feeling that people in general were untrustworthy or had hidden bad intentions toward you?

Doctor, I... I am honestly starting to get a little frustrated here. Are we going in circles? Is this some kind of test where you ask the exact same thing three different ways to see if I trip up and change my answer? Because my answer is still exactly the same. No. Never. Not at any point. 

I have never had a recurring pattern of thinking people were untrustworthy. I don't know how many other ways I can explain it to you. I mean, look at my personal life. I've been in the same bunco group—well, I say bunco, but it's really more of just a wine and gossip night now, we hardly ever actually bother rolling the dice anymore—but I've been getting together with those same four women on the second Thursday of every month since my daughter was in elementary school. If one of them cancels at the last minute, or if Linda forgets to bring the spinach dip she promised, I don't sit there spinning my wheels thinking she has some hidden bad intention or that she's secretly out to ruin my night. I just think, well, Linda's being flaky again, because Linda has always been a bit scattered. 

Or take my own brother, for instance. He's always asking to borrow a little money here and there, twenty bucks for gas, fifty bucks for groceries, you know how it is. I know he's just terrible with his finances. I do the billing at work, so I'm very organized, but he can't balance a checkbook to save his life. But when he asks for money, I don't think he's trying to bankrupt me on purpose or that he has some malicious master plan to drain my accounts. He's just my brother, and he's bad at math. 

I have always taken people at face value. If they are good to me, I am good to them. Up until nine months ago, I trusted basically everyone I interacted with. I really need us to move past this, Doctor, because I feel like I'm having to defend my entire personality and my whole past when the only issue—the absolute only issue—is what my husband's family is actively doing to me right now. Everything before that was completely, one hundred percent normal and trusting.
Before these past nine months, did you ever believe that people were plotting against you or trying to harm you in any other situations?

Doctor, I... I am really at a loss for words here. Are you even listening to me? I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall. How many times, honestly, how many different ways are you going to ask me the exact same question? 

No. No plotting. No harming. No other situations. 

Listen, let me give you an example, because I really need you to understand how completely normal my life has always been. When we lived in our old townhouse over on Maple Drive—this was years ago, my daughter was still in braces, so it had to be around two thousand and fourteen—we had this neighbor, a retired guy named Arthur. Arthur decided to put up a new privacy fence, one of those tall cedar ones, and the contractors he hired put the posts a good eight inches over onto our side of the property line. It was very obvious because it cut right into my hostas. 

Now, did I think Arthur was plotting against me? Did I think he was trying to steal my land or intentionally harm my garden because he had some vendetta against me? No, of course not! I didn't call the police or start thinking there was a neighborhood conspiracy. I just walked over there with a couple glasses of iced tea and I showed him the property survey we got when we closed on the house. And you know what? He apologized, he called the fence company, and they came back and moved it the very next day. 

That is how I handle things. I look at the facts, I look at the paperwork, just like I do with my invoices and spreadsheets at work. If there's a discrepancy, I point it out. I don't sit around inventing imaginary enemies or thinking people are plotting my downfall. 

So please, you have to stop asking me about my past like I've been walking around looking over my shoulder my whole entire life. I haven't. I was a completely normal, boring, everyday person until nine months ago. Nine months. That is the timeline. That is when his family started getting into my accounts and actively trying to ruin things for me. Why won't you ask me about that? Why do we keep digging into my past to find something that just isn't there when the actual problem is happening to me right now?
Before age 15, did you ever tend to be suspicious of other people or feel that they were untrustworthy?

Before age fifteen? Are you... I mean, seriously, Doctor? Now we are going all the way back to my childhood? I honestly feel like you are just pulling dates out of a hat now to see if I'll suddenly confess to being some lifelong paranoid hermit. 

No. Absolutely not. When I was a kid, I was probably the most naive, trusting little girl you could ever possibly meet. I was in the Girl Scouts until I was fourteen, for crying out loud. You don't go door-to-door selling thin mints to absolute strangers if you think people are inherently bad or untrustworthy. 

I remember when I was in seventh grade, so I would have been, what, twelve or thirteen? There was this girl in my homeroom, Jennifer Harding. She told me she forgot her lunch money for a whole week straight. And what did I do? I gave her half of my lunch and my extra snack money every single day. My mother always packed me these great lunches, usually a turkey and swiss on rye with a little bag of carrot sticks and a Little Debbie snack cake—the zebra cakes, those were my absolute favorite. And I just handed half of it over to Jennifer every day at noon because she said she was hungry. I didn't sit there at the cafeteria table thinking, "Oh, Jennifer is scamming me," or "Jennifer has a secret agenda to steal my food." I just thought the poor girl forgot her money! 

It actually turned out later that she was using her own lunch money to buy teen magazines at the pharmacy down the street, but even when I found that out, I didn't suddenly become suspicious of everyone else. I didn't stop trusting my other friends. I just thought Jennifer was a bit of a brat who owed me a zebra cake. That was it. 

I was a completely normal kid. I had sleepovers, I shared my locker with my best friend Stacy, I lent out my favorite clothes and never worried if I'd get them back. So no, not before I was fifteen, not in my twenties, not in my thirties, and not in my forties! Not until exactly nine months ago. 

I just... I don't understand what you are digging for here. Why is this so hard to get down on your notepad? The issue is my husband's family, right now, in the present day. Can we please, please talk about what they are actually doing to my bank accounts right now instead of interrogating me about middle school?
Outside of your husband’s family, have you ever felt that other people were generally untrustworthy?

I... I honestly don't know whether to laugh or cry right now. We are literally right back where we started. I feel like my head is going to spin right off my neck, Doctor. 

No. Outside of my husband's family? No, I have not. I really, truly have not.
